title: B2.3 Cell specialization
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: B2.3 Cell specialization — IB Diploma Programme Biology (guide first assessment 2025), topic B2.3.
meta_desc: IB DP Biology practice covering B2.3 Cell specialization, guide topic B2.3.
final_note: You worked through B2.3 Cell specialization — 10 guide statements.

concepts.def: The development of an unspecialized cell into a specialized cell with a particular structure and function. The cells produced by the early divisions of the zygote are unspecialized; differentiation happens when a cell expresses some of its genes and not others, so that it makes the proteins characteristic of one cell type. The genome is not changed: every differentiated cell keeps the full set of genes but uses only part of it.

A concentration gradient of a signalling chemical (a morphogen) across the early embryo, produced because the chemical is made or deposited in one region and spreads out from it. A cell's position in the gradient determines the concentration it experiences, and different concentrations switch on different genes, so cells in different positions express different genes and differentiate into different cell types.

An undifferentiated cell that has two defining properties: it can divide endlessly, producing more cells by mitosis without exhausting its capacity to divide, and it can differentiate along different pathways to produce specialized cell types.

A specific location in a tissue of an adult where stem cells are kept, and where signals from the surrounding cells and extracellular environment control what the stem cells do. The niche can maintain the stem cells in an undifferentiated, non-dividing state, or it can promote their proliferation and their differentiation into the cell types the tissue needs.

A niche in the red bone marrow inside bones where haematopoietic stem cells are maintained and, when signalled to, proliferate and differentiate to replace the blood cells (erythrocytes, white blood cells and platelet-producing cells) that are continually lost. It is one of the two example locations of adult stem cell niches used in this topic.

A niche in the bulge region of a hair follicle, below the skin surface, where stem cells are kept in a maintained state between hair growth cycles. When a new hair begins to grow, or the follicle is damaged, niche signals promote proliferation of the stem cells and their differentiation into the cells that build the new hair and its sheath.

A stem cell that can differentiate into any cell type of the organism, including the extra-embryonic cells that form the placenta and membranes around the embryo. The zygote and the cells of the very early embryo, up to the first few divisions, are totipotent.

A stem cell that can differentiate into any of the cell types of the body of the organism but not into the extra-embryonic tissues such as the placenta. Cells of an early-stage animal embryo soon lose totipotency and become pluripotent; the cells of the inner cell mass of the blastocyst are pluripotent embryonic stem cells.

A stem cell that can differentiate into only a limited range of cell types, typically the cell types of one tissue. Stem cells in adult tissues such as bone marrow are multipotent: bone marrow stem cells produce the different types of blood cell but not, for example, neurons or muscle.

concepts.term: Range of cell size in humans
concepts.def: Human cells vary in size by several orders of magnitude, and size is one aspect of a cell's specialization. A sperm cell has a head about 5 µm long and 3 µm wide, with a tail bringing its total length to about 50 µm; the egg cell is about 100 µm in diameter, the largest human cell by volume, because it stores cytoplasm and nutrients for the early embryo. Red blood cells are about 7–8 µm across; white blood cells are mostly larger, about 10–20 µm, although small lymphocytes are close to the size of a red blood cell. A neuron has a cell body of ordinary size but an axon that can be over a metre long, and a striated muscle fibre can be several centimetres long and 10–100 µm wide.

The surface area of a cell divided by its volume. As the linear size of a cell increases, its surface area increases with the square of the length but its volume increases with the cube, so the ratio falls. For a cube of side L the surface area is 6L², the volume is L³ and the ratio is 6/L.

The limit that surface area-to-volume ratio places on how large a cell can be. Exchange of materials (nutrients, oxygen, wastes, heat) across the cell surface depends on the area of that surface, whereas the need for exchange depends on the volume of cytoplasm carrying out metabolism. As a cell grows, its volume and its needs increase faster than its surface area, so beyond a certain size the surface can no longer supply the volume and the cell must stop growing, divide, or change shape.

concepts.term: Cube model of surface area-to-volume ratio
concepts.def: Cubes of different side lengths used as a simplified model of cells of different sizes. Doubling the side length multiplies the surface area by four and the volume by eight, so the ratio halves. The model is deliberately simpler than a real cell (NOS: models are simplified versions of complex systems), but the scale factors operate in the same way for any shape, so the conclusion that larger objects have smaller surface area-to-volume ratios applies to real cells.

An adaptation in which a cell is flattened so that no part of its cytoplasm is far from the surface, increasing the surface area-to-volume ratio and shortening diffusion distances. The erythrocyte is the example: it is a biconcave disc about 7–8 µm wide but only about 2 µm thick, so it has a much larger surface area than a sphere of the same volume, which speeds the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide.

Finger-like projections of the plasma membrane, each supported by cytoskeleton, that greatly increase the surface area of one face of a cell without adding much volume. Cells of the proximal convoluted tubule of the nephron have dense microvilli (a brush border) on the surface facing the tubule lumen, increasing the area of membrane available for reabsorbing glucose, ions, water and other useful substances from the filtrate.

Infolding of the plasma membrane into the cell, which increases the surface area without increasing the volume. Cells of the proximal convoluted tubule have deep invaginations of the membrane on their basal side, with mitochondria packed between the folds, increasing the area of membrane through which reabsorbed substances are transported out of the cell towards the blood.

The extremely thin, flattened cell that forms most of the surface of the alveolar epithelium. Its thinness, with the cytoplasm stretched into a very thin layer, minimizes the distance that oxygen and carbon dioxide must diffuse between the air in the alveolus and the blood in the capillaries.

A thicker, roughly cuboidal cell of the alveolar epithelium whose cytoplasm contains many secretory vesicles called lamellar bodies. The lamellar bodies discharge surfactant into the alveolar lumen, so that the alveolar surface is coated with surfactant.

concepts.term: Tissue with more than one cell type
concepts.def: A tissue in which two or more differently adapted cell types are present because no single cell type could carry out the overall function of the tissue. The alveolar epithelium is the example: gas exchange needs the extreme thinness of type I pneumocytes, while surfactant secretion needs the many lamellar bodies of type II pneumocytes, and one cell could not be both extremely thin and packed with secretory vesicles.

A contractile structure running the length of the cytoplasm of a muscle cell or fibre, made of repeating units of overlapping protein filaments whose sliding produces contraction. Myofibrils are present in both cardiac muscle cells and striated (skeletal) muscle fibres, and give both a striated appearance.

A relatively short, branched muscle cell of the heart wall containing myofibrils, usually with one nucleus (occasionally two). Cells are joined end to end where their branches meet, so that a network is formed. The hypothesis for the branching is that it lets contraction and the electrical signal that triggers it spread through the heart wall in all directions, so that the wall contracts as a coordinated unit.

A very long, unbranched, cylindrical unit of skeletal muscle containing many parallel myofibrils and many nuclei spread along its length. It is formed during development by the fusion of many separate cells (myoblasts). The hypothesis for its length is that a fibre spanning the length of a muscle can contract as one unit, and for its many nuclei that a single nucleus could not supply enough mRNA and protein for such a large volume of cytoplasm. Because it has one continuous plasma membrane and cytoplasm but arose from many cells, whether a striated muscle fibre is a cell or a multinucleate structure (syncytium) is a matter of debate.

concepts.term: Adaptations of the human sperm cell
concepts.def: A small, streamlined cell adapted to reach and enter the egg. It has a haploid nucleus in the head, an acrosome at the tip of the head containing enzymes that digest a path through the layers around the egg, a midpiece packed with mitochondria that supply ATP, and a long flagellum (tail) whose beating propels the cell. It has very little cytoplasm, so it is light and carries little to slow it down.

concepts.term: Adaptations of the human egg cell
concepts.def: A large, non-motile cell about 100 µm in diameter with a haploid nucleus and a large volume of cytoplasm containing stored nutrients (yolk droplets) that supply the embryo during its first divisions before it can obtain nutrients from the mother. It is surrounded by the zona pellucida, a layer of glycoproteins outside the plasma membrane that a sperm must penetrate, and it contains cortical granules beneath the membrane whose contents are released at fertilization to change the zona pellucida so that no further sperm can enter.

mcqs.q: In a human, a neuron and a liver cell are both descended by mitosis from the same zygote. What is the difference between them once they have differentiated?
options: They express different subsets of the same complete set of genes.
They have kept different sets of genes and discarded the rest.
They were set on different paths inside from fertilization.
They differ only until the body needs to swap them over.
mcqs.specStatementText: From one fertilized egg to many cell types
mcqs.explain: All cells produced by mitosis from the zygote inherit the full genome. Differentiation is a change in which genes are expressed: the neuron switches on the genes for its proteins and the liver cell switches on a different set, while both keep every gene.
rationales: All cells produced by mitosis from the zygote inherit the full genome. Differentiation is a change in which genes are expressed: the neuron switches on the genes for its proteins and the liver cell switches on a different set, while both keep every gene.

A student who thinks differentiation discards unneeded genes picks this. Gene content is unchanged by differentiation; only gene expression differs, and the silent genes remain in the nucleus of every specialized cell.

A student who believes cell fate is fixed internally in each cell from the start picks this. The early cells are unspecialized and identical; their fates are set later by their positions in gradients of signalling chemicals.

A student who thinks specialized cells can switch type on demand picks this. In the human body differentiation is effectively one-way; new cells of another type come from stem cells, not from conversion of differentiated cells.

mcqs.q: In an early-stage embryo a signalling protein is made by cells at one end and spreads towards the other end. Cells at three different distances from the source develop into three different cell types. Which explanation is best supported?
options: The protein is an on/off switch, so the cells that received it differ from the cells that did not.
Different genes are switched on above different concentrations, so each position expresses its own set.
Each cell's fate was fixed internally at fertilization; the protein only marks the region afterwards.
The protein removes different genes from cells at different distances, so each type keeps only the genes it needs.
mcqs.specStatementText: From one fertilized egg to many cell types
mcqs.explain: The protein forms a concentration gradient. Cells respond to the concentration they experience, with different genes switched on at different thresholds, so cells at high, medium and low concentration express different genes and differentiate into three types.
rationales: A student who treats a signal as present or absent picks this. An on/off switch could divide the embryo into two cell types only; three types at three distances show that cells respond to the level of the protein, not merely to its presence.

The protein forms a concentration gradient. Cells respond to the concentration they experience, with different genes switched on at different thresholds, so cells at high, medium and low concentration express different genes and differentiate into three types.

A student who thinks fate is programmed inside each cell from the start picks this. The cells are genetically identical and unspecialized; the gradient is what makes their gene expression differ, so the protein is a cause, not a label.
A student who thinks differentiation removes genes picks this. All the cells keep the whole genome; the gradient changes which genes are expressed at each position, not which genes are present.

mcqs.q: Which pair of properties defines a stem cell?
options: Ability to divide whenever a tissue is damaged and to produce more cells of its own type.
Ability to switch from one specialized type to another whenever a tissue requires this.
Capacity to divide endlessly and ability to differentiate along different pathways.
Continuous division at all times, giving new cells whether or not they are needed.
mcqs.specStatementText: What makes a cell a stem cell
mcqs.explain: These are the two defining properties in the guide: a stem cell can divide endlessly, and it can differentiate along different pathways to give specialized cell types. Both are required.
rationales: A student who thinks any cell that divides is a stem cell picks this. Differentiated cells such as fibroblasts divide during repair and produce their own type, but they have limited divisions and cannot differentiate along other pathways.

A student who thinks specialized cells are interchangeable picks this. A stem cell is undifferentiated; it produces other cell types by differentiating, not by converting one specialized type into another.
These are the two defining properties in the guide: a stem cell can divide endlessly, and it can differentiate along different pathways to give specialized cell types. Both are required.

A student who reads 'divide endlessly' as 'divide continuously' picks this. Stem cells have an unlimited capacity to divide but can be maintained in a resting state by their niche; the defining property is the capacity, not constant activity.

mcqs.q: In a hair follicle, stem cells in a region below the skin surface stay inactive for months between hair growth cycles. At the start of a new cycle they begin to divide and produce the cells of a new hair. What does this show about the stem cell niche?
options: It stores the stem cells, which decide on their own when to begin dividing.
It receives fresh stem cells sent from the bone marrow when a new hair is needed.
It converts ordinary dividing skin cells into stem cells at the start of each cycle.
It can maintain the stem cells or activate them, according to need.
mcqs.specStatementText: Niches: where adult stem cells live and who tells them what to do
mcqs.explain: A niche does two things: it can maintain stem cells in an undifferentiated resting state, and it can promote their proliferation and differentiation. The months of inactivity show maintenance; the start of a new cycle shows activation.
rationales: A student who pictures the niche as a storage shelf picks this. The stem cells respond to signals from the niche; the timing of activation at the start of a growth cycle is set by the niche environment, not by the cells acting independently.

A student who thinks adult stem cells exist only in bone marrow picks this. The hair follicle has its own resident stem cells in a niche below the skin surface; bone marrow stem cells supply blood cells, not hair.

A student who equates any dividing cell with a stem cell picks this. The follicle's stem cells are a maintained population of undifferentiated cells; differentiated skin cells that divide do not become stem cells.

A niche does two things: it can maintain stem cells in an undifferentiated resting state, and it can promote their proliferation and differentiation. The months of inactivity show maintenance; the start of a new cycle shows activation.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes pluripotent stem cells from totipotent stem cells?
options: Pluripotent cells can form any cell type of the body but not extra-embryonic tissues such as the placenta.
Pluripotent and totipotent cells can both form every cell type, so the two terms are interchangeable.
Pluripotent cells are the stem cells found in adult tissues such as bone marrow and hair follicles.
Pluripotent cells appear only after birth, since all the cells of an embryo remain totipotent.
mcqs.explain: Totipotent cells of the very early embryo can form every cell, including the placenta and membranes. Within a few divisions the cells become pluripotent: they can still form any body cell type but no longer the extra-embryonic tissues.
rationales: Totipotent cells of the very early embryo can form every cell, including the placenta and membranes. Within a few divisions the cells become pluripotent: they can still form any body cell type but no longer the extra-embryonic tissues.
A student who translates both prefixes as 'all' picks this. The terms differ precisely over the extra-embryonic tissues, which totipotent cells can form and pluripotent cells cannot.

A student who thinks adult stem cells can form any cell type picks this. Adult stem cells are multipotent, limited to the cell types of their own tissue; pluripotent cells are found in the early embryo.
A student who thinks embryonic cells stay totipotent throughout development picks this. Embryonic cells are totipotent only for the first few divisions and soon become pluripotent, well before birth.

mcqs.q: A cell taken from a 4-cell human embryo can develop into a complete individual with its own placenta. A cell from the inner cell mass of a blastocyst can form any tissue of the body but not a placenta. A stem cell from adult bone marrow forms only blood cells. How should the three cells be classified?
options: Totipotent for both embryo cells, then multipotent.
Totipotent, then pluripotent, then finally multipotent.
Totipotent, then pluripotent for both of the others.
Pluripotent for both embryo cells, then finally multipotent.
mcqs.explain: Forming a whole individual including the placenta is totipotency. Forming any body tissue but not the placenta is pluripotency. Forming only the cell types of one tissue, here blood, is multipotency.
rationales: A student who thinks all embryonic cells stay totipotent picks this. The inner cell mass cell cannot form the placenta, so it has already become pluripotent; totipotency is lost within the first few divisions.
Forming a whole individual including the placenta is totipotency. Forming any body tissue but not the placenta is pluripotency. Forming only the cell types of one tissue, here blood, is multipotency.
A student who believes adult stem cells can form any cell type picks this. The bone marrow cell forms only blood cells, which is the limited range that defines a multipotent stem cell.
A student who uses pluripotent and totipotent interchangeably picks this. A cell that can form the placenta as well as the embryo is totipotent; pluripotent cells cannot form extra-embryonic tissue.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the range of cell size in humans is correct?
options: Red and white blood cells and gametes are all about 10 µm across.
The egg and the sperm are similar in size, as each supplies half the DNA.
A motor neuron can be over a metre long, yet only micrometres wide.
A muscle fibre several centimetres long must be a chain of short cells.
mcqs.specStatementText: Human cells come in very different sizes
mcqs.explain: Cell size is an aspect of specialization. A single motor neuron running from the spinal cord to a muscle in the foot has an axon over a metre long, while its width remains microscopic; extreme length suits its function of carrying signals over a distance.
rationales: A student who assumes all cells are one generic size picks this. Red blood cells are 7–8 µm, white blood cells mostly about 10–20 µm, a sperm head about 5 µm and an egg about 100 µm across.

A student who carries the equal genetic contribution over to cell size picks this. The egg, about 100 µm across, is one of the largest human cells; the sperm is one of the smallest, because it carries almost no cytoplasm.

Cell size is an aspect of specialization. A single motor neuron running from the spinal cord to a muscle in the foot has an axon over a metre long, while its width remains microscopic; extreme length suits its function of carrying signals over a distance.

A student who thinks no single cell can be visible picks this. A striated muscle fibre is a single continuous unit with one plasma membrane that can run for centimetres; its length is part of its specialization.

mcqs.q: A cube of side 1 mm has a surface area of 6 mm², a volume of 1 mm³ and a surface area-to-volume ratio of 6. The side length is increased to 4 mm. What is the new surface area-to-volume ratio?
options: 6, because the surface area and the volume are both multiplied by four
24, because a larger cube has more surface, so the ratio rises fourfold
0.67, because it compares the 64 mm³ volume with the 96 mm² surface area
1.5, because the area becomes 96 mm² and the volume becomes 64 mm³
mcqs.specStatementText: Surface area against volume limits cell size
mcqs.explain: Surface area = 6 × 4² = 96 mm² and volume = 4³ = 64 mm³, so the ratio is 96 / 64 = 1.5. Multiplying the side by 4 multiplied the area by 16 and the volume by 64, so the ratio fell to a quarter of its original value.
rationales: A student who scales area and volume in direct proportion to length picks this. Area scales with the square of length (× 16) and volume with the cube (× 64), so the ratio does change: it falls to 1.5.
A student who confuses a larger surface area with a larger ratio picks this. The surface area does rise, to 96 mm², but the volume rises even faster, so the ratio falls from 6 to 1.5.

A student who divides the ratio the wrong way round picks this. The surface area-to-volume ratio is surface area divided by volume, 96 / 64 = 1.5; 64 / 96 is volume per unit area, which rises with size and hides the constraint.

Surface area = 6 × 4² = 96 mm² and volume = 4³ = 64 mm³, so the ratio is 96 / 64 = 1.5. Multiplying the side by 4 multiplied the area by 16 and the volume by 64, so the ratio fell to a quarter of its original value.

mcqs.q: A single-celled organism is growing. Why can it not keep growing indefinitely without dividing?
options: Its volume, which sets its need for exchange, grows faster than the surface through which exchange occurs.
Its surface area-to-volume ratio rises as it grows, until the membrane cannot hold the cell together.
Its larger surface area increases its need for materials until supply cannot keep up with demand.
Its surface area and volume increase by the same factor, so the limit must come from the nucleus instead.
mcqs.specStatementText: Surface area against volume limits cell size
mcqs.explain: The need for exchange of materials depends on the volume of cytoplasm, while the rate of exchange depends on the area of the surface. Volume increases with the cube of length and surface with the square, so demand outgrows supply and sets a limit on size.
rationales: The need for exchange of materials depends on the volume of cytoplasm, while the rate of exchange depends on the area of the surface. Volume increases with the cube of length and surface with the square, so demand outgrows supply and sets a limit on size.

A student who thinks the ratio increases with size picks this. The ratio falls as the cell grows, and the constraint is about supplying the cytoplasm with materials, not about the membrane failing mechanically.

A student who attaches the need for exchange to the surface picks this. Need is set by the volume of metabolizing cytoplasm; the surface is what supplies that need, and it is the surface that fails to keep up.

A student who scales area and volume in step picks this. They do not increase by the same factor: volume grows with the cube of length and surface area with the square, and it is this mismatch that constrains cell size.

mcqs.q: A student argues: 'Real cells are not cubes, so the cube model of surface area-to-volume ratio proves nothing about real cells.' Which response best evaluates this claim?
options: The claim is right: a model is only valid when it has the same shape as the thing that it represents.
The model is simplified on purpose; area and volume scale in the same way for any shape, so its conclusion holds.
The claim is right for another reason: in real cells the surface area and the volume grow in proportion.
The claim is wrong, because in real cells the ratio increases with size, which the simple cube model fails to show.
mcqs.specStatementText: Surface area against volume limits cell size
mcqs.explain: Models are simplified versions of complex systems. Cubes are simpler than real cells, but scaling a shape of any kind multiplies area by the square and volume by the cube of the scale factor, so the conclusion that larger cells have a smaller ratio applies to real cells.
rationales: A student who judges a model by its resemblance to the real thing picks this. The value of a model lies in the relationship it isolates, not in looking like the system; the cube model isolates the effect of size and does so correctly.

Models are simplified versions of complex systems. Cubes are simpler than real cells, but scaling a shape of any kind multiplies area by the square and volume by the cube of the scale factor, so the conclusion that larger cells have a smaller ratio applies to real cells.

A student who scales area and volume in step picks this. In any object, cube or cell, area grows with the square of length and volume with the cube, so they do not grow in proportion; the cube model shows exactly this.

A student who believes the ratio rises with size picks this. In real cells, as in cubes, the ratio falls as size increases; the cube model shows this correctly, which is why the claim is wrong for a different reason.

mcqs.q: A human erythrocyte has a volume of about 90 µm³ and a surface area of about 135 µm². A sphere with the same volume would have a surface area of about 97 µm². What do these figures show about the adaptation of the erythrocyte?
options: The biconcave shape gives it about 40% more room for haemoglobin than a sphere would provide.
The extra surface can only come from the erythrocyte being smaller than a typical sphere-shaped cell would be.
Flattening gives it about 40% more surface than a sphere of the same volume, which speeds gas exchange.
Its ratio of 1.5 is higher than the sphere's ratio of 1.08 because the erythrocyte is the larger of the two cells.
mcqs.explain: 135 / 97 ≈ 1.4, so the biconcave disc has about 40% more surface area than a sphere of equal volume, and its ratio (1.5) is higher than the sphere's (about 1.08). More surface and a shorter diffusion distance increase the rate at which oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged.
rationales: A student who thinks the shape is for holding more haemoglobin picks this. The comparison is between shapes of the same volume, 90 µm³, so there is no extra room; the flattened cell gains surface area, not internal space.

A student who thinks size is the only route to a high ratio picks this. The sphere in the comparison has exactly the same volume, so the extra surface comes from shape alone: flattening the cell adds area without adding volume.

135 / 97 ≈ 1.4, so the biconcave disc has about 40% more surface area than a sphere of equal volume, and its ratio (1.5) is higher than the sphere's (about 1.08). More surface and a shorter diffusion distance increase the rate at which oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged.
A student who thinks a larger cell has a larger ratio picks this. The two have the same volume, so neither is larger; and in any case a larger object has a smaller ratio, not a larger one.

mcqs.q: Which features of a proximal convoluted tubule cell increase its surface area-to-volume ratio, and how?
options: Microvilli, which beat to sweep the filtrate across the cell so that more of it can be absorbed.
A small cell size, because shape cannot alter the ratio of a cell that has a given volume.
Its large size, because a bigger cell has more surface and so a higher surface area-to-volume ratio.
Microvilli and basal invaginations, which add membrane area without adding volume.
mcqs.explain: Microvilli on the surface facing the filtrate and invaginations of the membrane on the basal side both extend the plasma membrane while the cell's volume stays the same, so the ratio rises and more membrane is available for reabsorption and transport to the blood.
rationales: A student who confuses microvilli with cilia picks this. Microvilli do not move; they are static folds of membrane whose only role here is to multiply the surface area for reabsorption.
A student who thinks only size affects the ratio picks this. Microvilli and invaginations show that shape does alter the ratio: they multiply the membrane area of a cell whose volume is unchanged.

A student who confuses a larger absolute surface area with a larger ratio picks this. A larger cell has a smaller ratio, because volume grows faster than surface area; proximal convoluted tubule cells raise their ratio by adding membrane (microvilli and invaginations), not by being large.

Microvilli on the surface facing the filtrate and invaginations of the membrane on the basal side both extend the plasma membrane while the cell's volume stays the same, so the ratio rises and more membrane is available for reabsorption and transport to the blood.

mcqs.q: How are type I and type II pneumocytes adapted to their functions in the alveolar epithelium?
options: Type I cells are extremely thin for a short diffusion distance; type II cells hold many lamellar bodies that discharge surfactant.
Type II cells are the thicker gas-exchange cells; type I cells are thin cells that line the gaps between them.
Type I cells secrete surfactant from their lamellar bodies; type II cells are thin to allow rapid diffusion.
Type I and type II cells are one cell type at two stages, with the thin type I cells maturing into type II cells.
mcqs.explain: Type I pneumocytes are stretched extremely thin so that gases diffuse only a short distance between alveolar air and blood. Type II pneumocytes contain many secretory vesicles, the lamellar bodies, which discharge surfactant into the alveolar lumen.
rationales: Type I pneumocytes are stretched extremely thin so that gases diffuse only a short distance between alveolar air and blood. Type II pneumocytes contain many secretory vesicles, the lamellar bodies, which discharge surfactant into the alveolar lumen.

A student who thinks the thicker, organelle-rich cell must do the main work picks this. Gas exchange depends on a short diffusion distance, so it is the extremely thin type I cells that form the exchange surface.

A student who has attached gas exchange to type II cells and swapped the roles picks this. It is type I cells that are extremely thin for diffusion and type II cells that contain the lamellar bodies that discharge surfactant.

A student who expects a tissue to contain a single cell type picks this. The alveolar epithelium contains two distinct cell types because thinness for diffusion and a cytoplasm full of secretory vesicles cannot both be built into one cell.

mcqs.q: A striated muscle fibre has one continuous plasma membrane and cytoplasm and contains hundreds of nuclei. Which is the best assessment of whether it is a cell?
options: It is not a cell, because a cell by definition contains exactly one nucleus, whereas this muscle fibre contains many hundreds.
It is debatable: one membrane and cytoplasm argue for a cell, but many nuclei and an origin by fusion argue for a syncytium.
It is a cell, because its nuclei arose by repeated mitosis inside a single cell that did not undergo cytokinesis.
It is a cell, because cardiac muscle cells also contain many nuclei, and they are accepted as cells by biologists.
mcqs.specStatementText: Cardiac muscle cells and striated muscle fibres (HL)
mcqs.explain: The guide asks for a discussion, not a verdict. A single membrane enclosing a single cytoplasm that works as a unit fits the idea of a cell; hundreds of nuclei and formation from many separate cells fit the idea of a multinucleate structure. Both positions can be defended.
rationales: A student who has made 'one nucleus' part of the definition of a cell picks this. Cell theory does not fix the number of nuclei; the nucleus count is one consideration in the debate, not a rule that settles it.

The guide asks for a discussion, not a verdict. A single membrane enclosing a single cytoplasm that works as a unit fits the idea of a cell; hundreds of nuclei and formation from many separate cells fit the idea of a multinucleate structure. Both positions can be defended.

A student who explains the many nuclei by mitosis without cytokinesis picks this. The fibre actually forms by fusion of many myoblasts, and that origin is the main argument against calling it a single cell.

A student who generalizes from skeletal to cardiac muscle picks this. Cardiac muscle cells are short, branched and usually have a single nucleus, so they offer no precedent for accepting a multinucleate fibre as a cell.

mcqs.q: A heart drug is found to block the passage of signals across the junctions where the branches of neighbouring cardiac muscle cells meet, without affecting the myofibrils inside each cell. Using the hypothesis for why cardiac muscle cells are branched, what effect on the heart wall would be predicted?
options: Contraction would still spread normally, because cardiac cells are fused into long multinucleate fibres, as in skeletal muscle.
Contraction would still be coordinated, because each cell is triggered by its own nerve ending, not its neighbours.
Contraction would no longer spread through the wall in all directions, so it would not contract as a coordinated unit.
Oxygen uptake would fall, because the junctions where branches meet are the extra surface through which the cells exchange materials.
mcqs.specStatementText: Cardiac muscle cells and striated muscle fibres (HL)
mcqs.explain: The hypothesis for branching is that it lets each cell connect with several neighbours, so the signal to contract, and the contraction itself, can pass through the network in every direction. If signals could not cross the junctions, each cell would contract in isolation and the wall would lose its coordinated contraction.
rationales: A student who assumes cardiac muscle is built like skeletal muscle picks this. Cardiac cells are short, separate and usually uninucleate; they are joined where their branches meet rather than fused, so a signal can only cross from one cell to the next through those junctions.

A student who thinks every muscle cell is stimulated separately by a nerve, as skeletal muscle fibres are, picks this. In the heart the signal to contract passes from cell to cell across the junctions between branches, so blocking those junctions would stop it spreading.

The hypothesis for branching is that it lets each cell connect with several neighbours, so the signal to contract, and the contraction itself, can pass through the network in every direction. If signals could not cross the junctions, each cell would contract in isolation and the wall would lose its coordinated contraction.

A student who explains every unusual cell shape as a way of increasing surface area-to-volume ratio picks this. The junctions are sites where the signal to contract passes between cells, not exchange surfaces; cardiac cells obtain oxygen from the capillaries around them, and the drug would affect coordination, not oxygen uptake.

mcqs.q: Which pairing correctly matches an adaptation of a human gamete to its function?
options: Sperm acrosome: stores the fuel that the mitochondria respire while the sperm swims.
Egg zona pellucida: a cell wall that gives the egg mechanical protection from damage.
Egg and sperm of matching size: each gamete carries half of the chromosomes needed.
Egg cytoplasm with nutrient stores: supplies the embryo's first divisions.
mcqs.specStatementText: Sperm and egg are built for different jobs (HL)
mcqs.explain: The egg is large because its cytoplasm contains stored nutrients (yolk droplets) that supply the embryo during its first divisions, before it can obtain nutrients from the mother. This is why the egg is one of the largest human cells.
rationales: A student who assumes the sperm carries a food store in its head picks this. The acrosome contains enzymes for digesting through the layers around the egg; the midpiece mitochondria respire substrates absorbed from the surrounding fluid.

A student who calls any layer outside the membrane a cell wall picks this. Animal cells have no cell wall; the zona pellucida is a glycoprotein layer that sperm bind to and digest through, then modified to block further sperm.

A student who links equal genetic contribution to equal size picks this. The gametes are extremely different in size: the egg is about 100 µm across and full of cytoplasm, while the sperm is tiny and streamlined for swimming.

scopeNotes.howHonoured: Stem cells are characterized only by the two properties the guide names: unlimited division and the capacity to differentiate along different pathways. Nothing is included on the molecular control of self-renewal, on asymmetric division, on induced pluripotent stem cells or on therapeutic uses of stem cells.

Only the two suggested niches, bone marrow and hair follicles, are used, and each is treated at the level of location plus the two things a niche can do: keep stem cells in an undifferentiated, maintained state, or signal them to proliferate and differentiate. No other niches (intestinal crypts, skin basal layer, neural niches) are named, and no named signalling molecules or niche cell types are required.

Type I pneumocytes are characterized only by their extreme thinness and its effect on diffusion distance; type II pneumocytes only by their many lamellar bodies that discharge surfactant into the alveolar lumen. The chemical composition of surfactant, its effect on surface tension and its role in ventilation are not tested here (they belong to B3.1), and nothing is included on the relative numbers or areas of the two cell types or on their capacity to replace each other after injury.

Only human sperm and human egg cells are described. No gametes of other animals, no plant gametes and no comparison of gamete types across species are included; the events of fertilization itself are left to D3.1 and only mentioned where they explain an adaptation of the gamete.
